{"self_assessment": "Impact: I laid the short stretch from the start down to the body, since nobody had claimed it and Maya's top curve grows from it. I also laid the bottom curve of the body, and later helped join the lower lobe to the tail edge. About 131 of 190 dominoes were dark at the push, so most of the fish should fall. I can't say yet whether the judge will read it as a fish. Two things could hurt us. My bottom curve looks like it stops short of the nose, so the outline may be open there. Some stray pieces are also still on the table, though they aren't connected to the start.

Execution: The body stayed pale for several minutes because of a gap at the junction below the start. I first tried bridging it, found the dominoes were already tight, and only then inspected. Priya spotted that the first body domino sat too far left, and I could have caught that sooner. I fixed it by relaying the top of the body from the start. After that I joined the lobe to the tail edge. Leo noted that a couple of dominoes there were crowded, and Priya confirmed the lobe was dark, so I stopped adding. I kept my hands off in the last minutes, which avoided bumps.

Collaboration: I announced what I was touching and where, and I asked Leo about his tail edge so we wouldn't steal each other's fall. I took Priya's and Leo's observations on board. I told Leo to take down the big loop on the right, since it wasn't mine. Staying clear of other people's work in the last two minutes helped us avoid bumps.

Leadership: Maya set the plan, and I backed it rather than competing. I took the unowned start stretch, kept status updates going, and called the hands-off point. I was less decisive on diagnosing the junction than I'd like, so my leadership was steady rather than standout."}
